BURSEVI:v10p183/r1.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p183/r1.speaker: فتح الرحمن
BURSEVI:v10p183/r1.claim: Fath al-Rahman treats the specification of dawn as an invitation to contemplate its marvels and the ordered regularity of its many motions.

BURSEVI:v10p183/r2.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p183/r2.speaker: أبو الليث
BURSEVI:v10p183/r2.claim: Abu al-Layth explains the moon in the preceding oath as the crescent after its third night.

BURSEVI:v10p183/r3.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p183/r3.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p183/r3.claim: The night and dawn clauses are coordinated with the moon; “when” is future-looking here because dawn follows night.

BURSEVI:v10p183/r4.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p183/r4.speaker: الراغب
BURSEVI:v10p183/r4.claim: Al-Raghib distinguishes safara, uncovering a physical covering, from asfara, which describes a color becoming clear and bright.

BURSEVI:v10p183/r5.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p183/r5.speaker: author
BURSEVI:v10p183/r5.claim: Asfara means that dawn brightens and clears; “pray at isfar” can mean entering the dawn time.

BURSEVI:v10p183/r6.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p183/r6.speaker: قوت القلوب
BURSEVI:v10p183/r6.claim: Qut al-qulub describes the second dawn as the sun’s white glow beneath the red twilight; sunset moves from red to white and darkness, while sunrise reverses that order before the sun’s disk appears.

BURSEVI:v10p183/r7.author: İsmāʿīl Ḥaqqī Bursevī
BURSEVI:v10p183/r7.speaker: الكاشفي
BURSEVI:v10p183/r7.claim: Kashifi reads the moon inwardly as a receptive, clear heart, the dark night as the lower self, and dawn as spirit-light that removes the heart’s darkness.

QASHANI:74:36/r2.author: ʿAbd al-Razzāq al-Qāshānī
QASHANI:74:36/r2.speaker: author
QASHANI:74:36/r2.claim: The moon is the receptive, clear heart; night is ego-darkness leaving as spirit-light splits through, and dawn is that light fully illuminating the heart.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p32/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p32/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p32/r4.claim: Nature’s manifestations argue for the Hereafter and expose heedlessness; the Qur’an warns so people can prepare, while evaders are left with stubbornness as their excuse.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r1.claim: The moon's slow phases answer why Judgment is delayed: humanity likewise advances through stages, and the Day comes at God's appointed time, when the universe's purpose is fulfilled.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r2.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r2.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r2.claim: The emphatic negation precedes the oath because the audience's denial is so objectionable that the speaker states rejection before giving its proof.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p53/r3.claim: Qur'anic oaths substantiate a following claim; here they answer disbelievers asking why the promised Judgment has not arrived yet.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r1.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r1.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r1.claim: The signs of God follow a prescribed plan; only He knows its benefits, and justice will appear at its appointed time despite demands for haste.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r3.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r3.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r3.claim: Night yielding to morning illustrates this world's darkness giving way to Judgment at its appointed time, as surely as daily dawn arrives.

ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r4.author: Amin Ahsan Islahi (d. 1997)
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r4.speaker: author
ISLAHI-TADABBUR:vol-9-english:p54/r4.claim: The daily alternation of night and dawn rehearses Judgment; nature continually supplies evidence of that Day for sincere truth-seekers.

QUSHAYRI:v3p364/r10.author: al-Qushayrī
QUSHAYRI:v3p364/r10.speaker: author
QUSHAYRI:v3p364/r10.claim: Asfara means that the morning has become clear and bright.

SULAMI:v2p359#4/r1.author: al-Sulamī
SULAMI:v2p359#4/r1.speaker: القاسم
SULAMI:v2p359#4/r1.claim: The dawn's brightening signifies the lights of spiritual illumination appearing in hearts.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r4.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r4.speaker: الحسن وأبو رزين وأبو رجاء وابن يعمر والسلمي وطلحة والأعمش ويونس بن عبيد ومطر
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r4.claim: A further reading uses idha and the hamzated adbara; its parallel with idha asfara is reflected in the codices of ʿAbd Allah and Ubayy.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r8.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r8.speaker: الجمهور
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r8.claim: The majority read asfara in the quadriliteral form.

ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r9.author: Abū Ḥayyān al-Gharnāṭī
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r9.speaker: ابن السميفع وعيسى بن الفضل
ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p335/r9.claim: They read the triliteral safara, meaning that dawn removes darkness from its face.

ALUSI-FULL:v29p130#2/r1.author: al-Ālūsī
ALUSI-FULL:v29p130#2/r1.speaker: author
ALUSI-FULL:v29p130#2/r1.claim: For the majority, أسفر means the morning became bright and clear; Ibn al-Sumayfi and Isa ibn al-Fadl read سفر in the triliteral form, meaning it removed darkness from its face.

BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p272/r3.author: al-Baghawī
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p272/r3.speaker: author
BAGHAWI-FULL:v8p272/r3.claim: The morning shines and becomes clear.

BIQAI-FULL:v8p233/r4.author: al-Biqāʿī
BIQAI-FULL:v8p233/r4.speaker: author
BIQAI-FULL:v8p233/r4.claim: The sunrise analogy depicts knowledge and guidance arriving as dawn illuminates and dispels confusion.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r6.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r6.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397/r6.claim: كلا rebukes disbelievers and rebels; the oaths by moon, night, and morning honor their signs and direct reflection toward God, who sustains all existence.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397#2/r14.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397#2/r14.speaker: author
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397#2/r14.claim: أسفر means that dawn brightens and spreads its light before sunrise.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397#2/r15.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397#2/r15.speaker: عيسى بن الفضيل وابن السميفع
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397#2/r15.claim: They read إذا أسفر, as if morning casts darkness off its face; Abu Hatim considers this weak.

IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397#2/r16.author: Ibn ʿAṭiyya
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397#2/r16.speaker: أبو علي الفارسي
IBNATIYYA-FULL:v5p397#2/r16.claim: Abu Ali al-Farisi considers both readings of أدبر sound.

IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p410/r1.author: Ibn al-Jawzī
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p410/r1.speaker: author
IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v8p410/r1.claim: Asfara means that dawn has brightened and become clear.

JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r6.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r6.speaker: ابن السميقع
JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r6.claim: Ibn al-Sumayqa reads waṣ-ṣubḥ idh safara without alif; safara and asfara are both valid words for becoming bright, possibly from a woman uncovering her face.

JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r10.author: al-Ḥākim al-Jishumī
JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r10.speaker: author
JISHUMI:v10p7165#2/r10.claim: Isfār means appearance and becoming visible; the cited verse uses sufūr for a woman's appearing without her veil.

SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r8.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r8.speaker: عيسى بن الفضل وابن السميفع
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r8.claim: The common reading has the quadriliteral ‘asfara’; ‘Isa ibn al-Fadl and Ibn al-Sumayfi read the triliteral ‘safara’.

SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r9.author: al-Samīn al-Ḥalabī
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r9.speaker: author
SAMIN-DURR:74:33-34/r9.claim: ‘Asfara’ means that dawn has cast darkness from its face, expressed as a metaphor.

MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r15.author: al-Māwardī
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r15.speaker: author
MAWARDI-FULL:v6p145/r15.claim: The morning when it brightens is a third object of the oath.

NASAFI-FULL:v4p297#3/r1.author: al-Nasafī
NASAFI-FULL:v4p297#3/r1.speaker: author
NASAFI-FULL:v4p297#3/r1.claim: Asfar means that dawn became bright; the oath's answer follows.

QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r11.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r11.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r11.claim: Asfara means that morning light brightened; the common reading has the alif, while Ibn al-Sumayqa reads safara, another dialectal form.

QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r12.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r12.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r12.claim: The Prophet’s instruction to delay the dawn prayer until it brightens is explained as praying after the light appears or lengthening prayer until sunrise approaches.

QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r13.author: al-Qurṭubī
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r13.speaker: author
QURTUBI-FULL:74:32-35/r13.claim: The word may describe a face shining or a woman uncovering her face; it may also derive from sweeping away darkness, as a broom clears a house.

RAZI-FULL:v30p184/r1.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI-FULL:v30p184/r1.speaker: author
RAZI-FULL:v30p184/r1.claim: Asfara means 'became bright'; the prophetic instruction to pray fajr asfira uses the same sense, as does describing faces as radiant in 80:38.

STUDYQURAN:74:32/r1.author: Seyyed Hossein Nasr (ed.-in-chief), Caner K. Dagli, Maria Massi Dakake, Joseph E. B. Lumbard, Mohammed Rustom
STUDYQURAN:74:32/r1.speaker: Āl, Ṭ
STUDYQURAN:74:32/r1.claim: “Nay” rejects claims that people can know God’s hosts’ number or overcome them; the oath also recalls other oaths on the moon and the night-day alternation.

TAB-FULL:v23p443/r1.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p443/r1.speaker: author
TAB-FULL:v23p443/r1.claim: The morning is brightening; Qatāda says it has become bright and is arriving.

TAB-FULL:v23p443/r2.author: al-Ṭabarī
TAB-FULL:v23p443/r2.speaker: قتادة
TAB-FULL:v23p443/r2.claim: Qatāda glosses dawn as brightening and coming on.

TABATABAI:74:35-38/r4.author: Muḥammad Ḥusayn al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī
TABATABAI:74:35-38/r4.speaker: author
TABATABAI:74:35-38/r4.claim: The oath pairs night retreat with its opposite, the morning's unveiling; idbar is the reverse of the night's arrival, and isfar is the clearing of dawn.

TABRISI:74:36-37/r9.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:74:36-37/r9.speaker: قتادة
TABRISI:74:36-37/r9.claim: The morning is sworn by when it lights up and shines.

TABRISI:74:36-37/r10.author: al-Ṭabrisī
TABRISI:74:36-37/r10.speaker: author
TABRISI:74:36-37/r10.claim: Alternatively, morning shines by clearing darkness and revealing visible objects; some interpret the oaths as being by the Lord of these things, since an oath may only be made by God.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p445/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p445/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p445/r1.claim: Asfara means dawn brightened and became clear; the hadith instruction to wait for dawn prayer means praying once its light is evident and doubt is removed.

WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p445/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p445/r2.speaker: author
WAHIDI-BASIT:v22p445/r2.claim: The same word describes faces shining on the Day of Resurrection.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:74:32-39/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:74:32-39/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:74:32-39/r3.claim: Dawn “when it brightens” means it becomes luminous.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:74:32/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:74:32/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:74:32/r1.claim: The oaths by the moon, departing night, and dawning morning draw attention both to divine signs and to the importance of the warning to humanity.
